content:
The headshot you need before a job interview is your LinkedIn photo, and you need it before you apply, not after. The interviewer will look you up, form a first impression from that photo in a fraction of a second, and then check it against the person who walks in. So the job is simple: make it recent, make it clear, and make it look exactly like you.

That last part matters more than any styling choice. A photo that is a flattering upgrade on the real you does not impress anyone in the room. It makes them wonder what else on the CV was polished.

What headshot do you need before a job interview?

A recent head and shoulders photo, evenly lit, in the outfit you would interview in, that reads as you within a second. It lives on LinkedIn, because that is where a hiring manager, recruiter or future teammate will find you before the interview. Members with a photo get up to 21 times more profile views according to LinkedIn Sales Solutions, and the photo is the first thing judged.

Fix it in the week before you apply, and the interview starts on the right foot.

Will the interviewer look at my LinkedIn before the interview?

Assume yes. Anyone who has your name and a calendar invite has a reason to check who they are about to meet, and LinkedIn is the first result for most professionals. If the profile has no photo, or an old one, that is the version of you they carry into the room.

LinkedIn's own numbers show how much the photo does for you: profiles with a photo get up to 21 times more views and 9 times more connection requests, per LinkedIn Sales Solutions. Those are views from people deciding whether you are worth a conversation. Before an interview, that is exactly the audience you want to reach.

How fast is the first impression formed?

Faster than the interviewer can read your headline. Princeton research by Willis and Todorov found that people judge trustworthiness, competence and likeability from a face after about 100 milliseconds. Looking longer mostly made them more confident in the verdict they had already reached.

So by the time your experience is being read, the photo has already set the tone. That is not a reason to panic. It is a reason to give the photo the same care you gave the cover letter, because it is doing more of the talking.

Does the photo need to match the person in the room?

Yes, and this is where a lot of people get it wrong in the other direction. LinkedIn's profile photo guidelines require the photo to reflect your likeness, and that is also the practical test an interviewer applies. They compare the photo in their head with the person shaking their hand.

A "better" version of you, with a slimmer face, smoother skin or a jaw you do not have, costs trust at the door. The gap between the picture and the person becomes the first thing they notice, and they notice it before you say a word.

Ten years younger is the same problem. Recent and honest beats polished and slightly off, every time.

What should I fix in the week before the interview?

Four things, in order of how much they change the result.

  1. Recent. Taken in the last year or two, with your current hair, glasses and weight. If you have changed, the photo has to change.
  2. Head and shoulders. LinkedIn shows the photo small and in a circle. A close crop keeps your face readable at that size.
  3. Even light. Face a window in daylight. No hard shadows under the eyes, no overhead office lighting, no flash.
  4. The outfit you would interview in. If it is a suit, wear the suit. If it is a collared shirt or a smart knit, wear that. The photo should look like the same person on the same day.

Then the check that ties it together: show the photo to a colleague and ask if it looks like you on a normal day. If they hesitate, retake it.

Pre-interview headshot checklist

  • The LinkedIn photo is under two years old and shows your current look.
  • It is cropped head and shoulders, with a little space above your head.
  • The light on your face is even, with no heavy shadows or filters.
  • You are wearing what you will wear to the interview, or something equally formal.
  • Someone who knows you has confirmed it looks like you in person.

Work through those five before you send the application. The photo is the one part of your first impression you can fully control, so control it.

faqs.question: Should I update my LinkedIn photo before applying for a job?
faqs.answer: Yes, before you apply, not after the interview is booked. Recruiters and hiring managers look at your profile as soon as your name reaches them, and the photo is the first thing they judge. An old or missing photo is the version of you they carry into the room.

faqs.question: Does my LinkedIn headshot need to look like me in person?
faqs.answer: Yes. LinkedIn requires the photo to reflect your likeness, and interviewers compare the photo with the person who walks in. A photo that is noticeably younger, slimmer or smoother than you costs trust at the door, so recent and honest beats polished and slightly off.

faqs.question: What should I wear in a headshot for a job interview?
faqs.answer: Whatever you would wear to the interview itself. If the role calls for a suit, wear the suit in the photo, and if it is a collared shirt or smart knit, wear that. The aim is for the photo and the handshake to look like the same person on the same day.
